item.title: [Biomedicine #1] Unbiased niche labeling maps immune-excluded niche in bone metastasis
item.dc:creator: Authors not captured in RSS
item.description: Unbiased niche labeling maps immune-excluded niche in bone metastasis Authors not captured in RSS · Cell · 2026-04-27 · research article Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: An unbiased niche-labeling method, SAMENT, maps cellular and molecular features of metastatic niches and highlights the role of ERα⁺ niche macrophages in preventing T cell infiltration, thereby promoting bone metastasis. Why it matters: Bone metastasis is notoriously resistant to immunotherapy. Identifying the specific macrophage subset (ERα⁺) that enforces immune exclusion provides a concrete mechanistic target for combination strategies aimed at converting cold bone metastases to immune-infiltrated. Why for Yiru: Directly maps to tumor microenvironment, macrophage biology, T cell exclusion, and translational cancer immunotherapy — with a spatial niche methodology that complements spatial omics interests.

item.title: [Biomedicine #2] ErbB family receptor dimerization dynamics and dysregulation via long-term single-molecule imaging
item.dc:creator: Ma et al.
item.description: ErbB family receptor dimerization dynamics and dysregulation via long-term single-molecule imaging Ma et al. · Cell · 2026-04-27 · research article Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: Ma et al. developed long-term single-particle tracking of ErbB family receptors in living cells using upconverting nanoparticles. They discovered constitutive HER2 and HER3 homodimerization and showed how oncogenic mutations and ligand stimulation affect dimerization dynamics, offering new insights into the mechanisms of oncogenic signaling and the ErbB receptor interaction network. Why it matters: ErbB/HER family signaling drives many cancers, yet the dynamic dimerization behavior of these receptors in living cells has been poorly understood. Single-molecule resolution of constitutive dimerization and mutation-driven dysregulation refines the mechanistic model of oncogenic signaling and could inform therapeutic design. Why for Yiru: Relevant to cancer biology and oncogenic signaling, with a cutting-edge live-cell single-molecule methodology angle. The receptor network systems-view resonates with computational modeling interests.

item.title: [Computational #1] Interpretable, flexible and spatially aware integration of multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets from diverse sources
item.dc:creator: Jia Zhao et al.
item.description: Interpretable, flexible and spatially aware integration of multiple spatial transcriptomics datasets from diverse sources Jia Zhao et al. · Nature Genetics · 2026-04-27 · research article DOI: 10.1038/s41588-026-02579-x Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: INSPIRE combines deep learning with non-negative matrix factorization to integrate diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets, recovering shared and context-specific spatial gene programs and tissue organization across scales. Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics technologies have enabled tissue-level gene expression profiling, but integrating datasets from different platforms, species, and experimental conditions remains challenging due to batch effects, differing gene panels, and varying spatial resolutions. INSPIRE addresses these challenges by combining deep learning with non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to learn interpretable, spatially-aware latent representations. The model decomposes gene expression into shared and context-specific spatial programs, enabling cross-dataset comparison of tissue organization while preserving biological interpretability. Why it matters: Cross-platform spatial integration is a central bottleneck. INSPIRE's interpretable factorization is a strong alternative to black-box embeddings when biological programs must be compared across cohorts. Why for Yiru: Directly aligned with spatial transcriptomics methods, multi-sample integration, and interpretable representation learning for tissue organization.

item.title: [Computational #2] Dango: Predicting higher-order genetic interactions
item.dc:creator: Ruochi Zhang et al.
item.description: Dango: Predicting higher-order genetic interactions Ruochi Zhang et al. · Cell Systems · 2026-04-24 · research article Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: DANGO uses a self-attention hypergraph neural network integrating multimodal molecular networks and protein sequence embeddings to predict higher-order genetic interactions, expanding the yeast trigenic interaction landscape to over 400 million interactions. Why it matters: Higher-order interactions are combinatorially intractable to measure; predictive graph models make perturbation landscapes computationally navigable. Why for Yiru: Representation learning on biological graphs, perturbation modeling, and computational functional genomics — strong overlap with method interests.

item.title: [Computational #3] Learning multi-cellular representations of single-cell transcriptomics data enables characterization of patient-level disease states
item.dc:creator: Tianyu Liu et al.
item.description: Learning multi-cellular representations of single-cell transcriptomics data enables characterization of patient-level disease states Tianyu Liu et al. · Cell Systems · 2026-03-31 · research article Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: PaSCient learns sample-level representations from single-cell RNA-seq across disease and tissue contexts, highlighting cells and genes that predict patient-level phenotypes such as disease severity and drug response. Why it matters: Single-cell foundation models operate at cell level, but clinical translation requires patient-level representations. This directly addresses that scale mismatch. Why for Yiru: Bridges single-cell modeling, biomedical AI, and translational disease stratification — a key direction for computational immunology applications.

item.title: [Biomedicine #1] Spatial 5mC-seq profiling of embryos and decidua after implantation in mammals
item.dc:creator: Xun Shan et al.
item.description: Spatial 5mC-seq profiling of embryos and decidua after implantation in mammals Xun Shan et al. · Nature Methods · 2026-04-27 · research article DOI: 10.1038/s41592-026-03079-w Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: Spatial 5mC-seq enables unbiased spatiotemporal genome-wide methylome profiling at single-cell resolution in mammalian embryos and decidua. Why it matters: Expands spatial omics beyond transcript measurements into the methylome, opening a new axis for linking cell state with spatial context. Why for Yiru: High-impact spatial method that broadens the toolkit beyond RNA/protein readouts — relevant for multi-omics spatial analysis.

item.title: [Biomedicine #2] Reference-free discovery with barcoded single-cell sequencing
item.dc:creator: Jacob M. Musser et al.
item.description: Reference-free discovery with barcoded single-cell sequencing Jacob M. Musser et al. · Nature Biotechnology · 2026-04-22 · research article DOI: 10.1038/s41587-026-03084-6 Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: sc-SPLASH extends reference-free analysis to barcoded single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data, reducing dependence on fixed annotations and prior marker sets. Why it matters: Reference-free discovery is essential when annotations are incomplete or biased — a recurring limitation in exploratory single-cell and spatial analyses. Why for Yiru: Methodologically relevant: robust discovery from barcoded single-cell and spatial data without relying on predefined references.

item.title: [Biomedicine #3] Sialylated CD43 forms a glyco-immune barrier that restrains antileukemic immunity
item.dc:creator: Authors not specified in RSS
item.description: Sialylated CD43 forms a glyco-immune barrier that restrains antileukemic immunity Authors not specified in RSS · Science · 2026-04-09 · research article DOI: 10.1126/science.ady5196 Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: CRISPR knockout screens in human AML cells identify sialylated CD43 as a glyco-immune barrier that restrains macrophage-mediated antileukemic immunity. Why it matters: Macrophage-directed immunotherapy has struggled clinically; a specific tumor glycosylation barrier provides a concrete mechanism and intervention axis. Why for Yiru: Strong match for tumor microenvironment, macrophage biology, and translational cancer immunotherapy — with a CRISPR screen methodology angle.

item.title: [Biomedicine #4] A convergent uPAR-positive tumor ecosystem creates broad vulnerability to CAR T cell therapy
item.dc:creator: Zeda Zhang et al.
item.description: A convergent uPAR-positive tumor ecosystem creates broad vulnerability to CAR T cell therapy Zeda Zhang et al. · Cell · 2026-03-30 · research article Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: uPAR CAR T cells synergize with senescence-inducing therapies to eradicate primary and metastatic solid tumors by targeting both tumor cells and supportive stroma, with minimal myelodepletion. Why it matters: Solid-tumor CAR T needs targets that capture tumor and stromal compartments; a convergent ecosystem vulnerability suggests broader efficacy than tumor-cell-only antigens. Why for Yiru: Directly maps to CAR-T, tumor microenvironment, and translational cancer biology interests.

item.title: [Biomedicine #5] Global genetic interaction network of a human cell maps conserved principles and informs functional interpretation of gene co-essentiality profiles
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Billmann et al.
item.description: Global genetic interaction network of a human cell maps conserved principles and informs functional interpretation of gene co-essentiality profiles Maximilian Billmann et al. · Cell · 2026-04-27 · research article Recommendation: READ FULL Summary: CRISPR perturbation of ~4 million gene pairs in human HAP1 cells maps ~89,000 genetic interactions, revealing a hierarchical network linking genes to complexes, pathways, and cellular processes while elucidating cancer cell dependencies. Why it matters: A human-scale genetic interaction map is a foundational resource for interpreting co-essentiality, pathway structure, and synthetic vulnerability. Why for Yiru: Systems-level reference for perturbation biology and computational interpretation of cancer dependencies — complements the computational methods in this digest.

item.title: [Other Fields #1] Today's robots walk, swim, fly, and manipulate objects on the go — and they're just getting started
item.dc:creator: Science Robotics Editors
item.description: Today's robots walk, swim, fly, and manipulate objects on the go — and they're just getting started Science Robotics Editors · Science · 2026-04-16 · review DOI: 10.1126/science.aeg9576 Recommendation: SKIM Summary: Recent advances in AI-driven control systems have enabled robots to transition between rolling, walking, flying, and swimming — and to use legs as manipulators while moving. This review covers the control challenges overcome to achieve multi-modal locomotion. Why it matters: Multi-modal robots represent a convergence of AI, control theory, and mechanical engineering — a milestone toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. Why for Yiru: A clean AI + robotics breakthrough with no biomedical angle. Tracks how AI is transforming physical systems outside the life sciences.

item.title: [Other Fields #2] AIs can 'memorize' data they shouldn't. Can they be forced to forget?
item.dc:creator: Science News Staff
item.description: AIs can 'memorize' data they shouldn't. Can they be forced to forget? Science News Staff · Science · 2026-04-06 · research news Recommendation: SKIM Summary: A new tool helps researchers probe how large language models 'unlearn' sensitive training material, addressing a core tension between model capability and data privacy. Why it matters: Machine unlearning is becoming a practical requirement as models are trained on increasingly broad data. This work addresses a key AI safety and privacy challenge. Why for Yiru: A fundamental AI safety research topic — relevant to anyone working with or thinking about foundation models, without being tied to biomedicine.

item.title: [Other Fields #3] Higher education must bridge the AI gap
item.dc:creator: Science Editorial
item.description: Higher education must bridge the AI gap Science Editorial · Science · 2026-04-02 · editorial DOI: 10.1126/science.aeh5777 Recommendation: SKIM Summary: As AI advances at a pace that outstrips regulatory and ethical frameworks, this editorial argues that higher education must develop students who can critically engage with AI systems rather than merely use them. Why it matters: The AI literacy gap in higher education affects how the next generation of scientists and engineers will interact with AI — a structural challenge that shapes all fields. Why for Yiru: A cross-cutting AI policy and education perspective — relevant to academic career planning and the evolving role of AI in scientific training.
